output.brief: The evidence points to the merit scholarship cut, not the Admissions Office, as the main driver of the drop. Yield fell from 41.8% to 34.3%. It fell only in the tiers where awards were cut: Dean's from 45.2% to 31.9% and Merit from 44.9% to 32.3%. Presidential awards were unchanged and yield was flat at about 36%. Students with no merit award barely moved, from 38.5% to 37.0%. Early-action yield fell almost as much as regular-decision yield (45.2% to 37.8% versus 39.0% to 31.5%). Early-action decisions were on time on the old system, so slow regular-decision turnaround doesn't explain the drop. Applications and admit quality rose, so a weaker applicant pool isn't the cause either. The slow portal and the reader cuts were real, and the Westcombe counsellor's complaint shows they cost individual students. They don't account for the 330-student gap. Replacing the director on this basis would punish the wrong party. I'd recommend taking a proposal to the finance committee to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers, with the net-revenue trade-off modelled. Also set a monthly-reported turnaround target for regular decision, and check the missing-transcript complaints before ordering any portal rebuild. Confidence is fairly high on the scholarship finding. The tier data can't fully separate the price effect from other influences.
